slides: Open by naming the chapter's central problem: ordinary functions do not carry their own coordinate-change rule, but top-degree forms do. The lecture moves from local signed volume to global integration, then to Stokes, corners, Riemannian volume, and densities.

Use the dependency map as the chapter route. Signed volume feeds Euclidean form integration, pullbacks explain change of variables, partitions of unity assemble local chart pieces, and Stokes connects exterior derivative with boundary. The graph also shows why orientation failure leads naturally to densities.

A top-degree form is a signed volume meter. In the notebook's two-vector sample, dx wedge dy evaluates to 1.5325 on (u,v), to -1.5325 after swapping the vectors, and to zero on a dependent pair. This is the algebraic behavior integration needs.

This slide explains why forms know the change-of-variables formula internally. For the map G(u,v)=(u+v/5,v), the determinant is one, and both the substituted integral and the pullback integral are 23/12. The residual is zero because the Jacobian factor is part of the pullback.

The partition of unity slide is the local-to-global construction. Compactly supported forms are split into chart-supported pieces, integrated locally, and added. The toy model has two equal chart contributions, 0.9045568434251863 each, assembling exactly to the whole integral 1.8091136868503725.

Present Stokes as the conceptual center of the chapter. On the rectangle, omega equals -y/2 dx plus x/2 dy, so d omega is dx wedge dy. The top and right boundary pieces each contribute a*b/2, and the boundary total equals the area integral a*b.

Corners require bookkeeping, not a new integral on the corner points. In the square divergence model, the vector field (x^2,y^2) has divergence 2x+2y, the two outgoing positive edges contribute one each, and the total flux equals the divergence integral two.

A Riemannian metric supplies a positive local volume density sqrt(det g). On an oriented manifold this can be read as a volume form, but without orientation the density still integrates because it keeps absolute size. The sample density stays positive under orientation-preserving, orientation-reversing, and Mobius-loop transitions.

Use the learner lab as the practical decision point. If a chart transition reverses orientation, a top form changes sign, while a density keeps multiplier one. That is why oriented form integration and nonorientable density integration are related but not interchangeable.

Close by tying each artifact to the theorem it supports. The determinant measures signed volume, pullback carries the Jacobian, partitions assemble local pieces, Stokes turns d into a boundary operator, corners cancel in lower codimension, and densities keep integration available when orientation fails.
